extracted.intended_audience: orators, writers, and students of rhetoric and literary style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing elevated, impassioned, and 'sublime' prose/poetry using rhetorical figures and diction; evaluates when to use devices (questions, asyndeton, hyperbaton, metaphors, periphrasis, etc.) and trade-offs between loftiness and faultlessness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of question and interrogation
rubrics_metrics.description: The figures of question and interrogation possess a specific quality which tends strongly to stir an audience and give energy to the speaker's words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate question and answer (or reply to oneself) to mimic meeting objections and reproduce the moment of passion; makes words more convincing and appears spontaneous, 'strikes our mental eye' and 'deceives' the audience into believing inspiration rather than labor produced the utterance. Example passages cited (Phil., Herodotus). Anti-pattern: putting such material 'baldly' would lose force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of connecting particles (Asyndeton)
rubrics_metrics.description: The removal of connecting particles gives a quick rush and 'torrent rapture' to a passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sever words without stops to give a lively impression of one who halts and hurries in speech; examples: Xenophon ('Clashing their shields together they pushed, they fought, they slew, they fell') and Homer. Use when you want rapidity and urgency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of different figures
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination of different figures, when two or three uniting their resources mutually contribute, is highly conducive to energy, vigour, cogency, and beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine repetition, broken clauses, inversions etc. to preserve intrinsic force and avoid stillness; example: Demosthenes' passage repeating and breaking sentences to imitate action. Vary movement continually so irregularity attains a measure of order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid smoothing passion with excessive conjunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjunctions and logical connecting links curb passion's free rush and smooth away the rapidity and rugged abruptness of passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare broken, rapid forms (which convey passion) with Isocrates' logical sequence which 'disappears' the point and fire of the passage. Use fewer conjunctions to preserve passionate effect; don't 'bind two runners together.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of hyperbaton (transposition) to imitate agitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyperbaton = transposition of words or thoughts from their usual order, bearing the stamp of violent mental agitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transpose address, invert logical order, leave thoughts in suspense and insert extraneous matters to make the hearer fear breakdown and thus share the speaker's peril; Thucydides, Demosthenes make bold use. Use to give impression of unpremeditated, crisis-driven speech; overuse is possible — examples are plentiful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juxtaposition, enumeration, contrast, and climax
rubrics_metrics.description: The juxtaposition of different cases, the enumeration of particulars, and the use of contrast and climax add much vigour, beauty, and elevation to style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change case/time/person/number/gender as needed to increase diversity and movement. Use lists and contrast to heighten effect; apply where the theme allows amplification and passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of plural for singular to amplify (expansion of number)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plurals for singulars sometimes fall with more impressive dignity, rousing imagination by the mere sense of vast number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ plural forms to give impression of multiplied calamity or pomp (examples: Oedipus lines; 'There came forth Hectors, and there came Sarpedons'). Restrict this device to themes that allow amplification; avoid over-ornamenting every sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contraction of plurals into singulars for dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Contraction of many particulars into a singular word can create an appearance of great dignity (e.g., 'all Peloponnesus was divided' instead of listing spectators).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when knitting together scattered particulars into one corporate whole gives them an aspect of corporate life; employ to give sudden change of complexion to circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrating past events as present (dramatic present)
rubrics_metrics.description: When past events are introduced as happening in present time the narrative form changes into dramatic action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use present-tense narration to make readers spectators rather than readers (examples: Xenophon, Thucydides) and to heighten immediacy and drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interchange of persons and direct personal address
rubrics_metrics.description: Interchange of persons and addressing the individual reader places the reader amidst the scene and excites interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address 'thou' or a specific individual to rouse interest, fix attention, and make the reader a partaker in the action (examples from poetry and Herodotus). Use to transform reader into spectator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sudden transition from third to first person
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer may suddenly step aside in a third-person narrative and transition to the first as an outburst of passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effect is striking and mimics an urgent crisis; avoid prefacing with tags like 'he said' which would have a frigid effect. Use this figure for urgent moments that 'will not allow the writer to linger.' Example: Hector's abrupt threat in the Iliad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periphrasis (circumlocution) to add dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Periphrasis tends to sublimity: it harmonises simple expressions by investing them with melody and dignity (e.g., calling death 'the destined journey').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend periphrastic turns agreeably with literal expression; avoid inflated or harsh periphrasis. Use to lend wider, loftier sentiment to eulogies and solemn topics; anti-pattern: using grand periphrasis for trifling subjects ('huge tragic mask on a little child').

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of appropriate and striking words
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of appropriate and striking words has a marvellous power and enthralling charm; beautiful words are the very light of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match diction to occasion — beautiful words endow facts with a vocal soul, but imposing language is not appropriate to every occasion. Avoid dressing trivial subjects in stately words; aim for aptness and expressiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of homely/plain language for vividness
rubrics_metrics.description: The most homely language is sometimes far more vivid than the most ornamental, being recognised as the language of common life and gaining immediate currency by its familiarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't shy from simple, familiar phrasing when it conveys vividness (examples: Theophrastus phrase about Philip 'taking doses of trouble'; Herodotus' blunt depictions). Balance ornament with homely expressiveness where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of metaphors — moderation vs occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Some critics advise limiting metaphors to two or three in the same place, but the use must be determined by the occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In outbursts of passion many metaphors may be indispensable; in calmer contexts limit metaphors. Soften harsh metaphors with phrases like 'so to say' or 'if I may be permitted the expression' to forestall criticism. Strong feeling and unaffected sublimity can naturally counterbalance daring metaphorical use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of metaphors in descriptive and familiar topics
rubrics_metrics.description: A close and continuous series of metaphors gives distinctness in treating familiar topics and in descriptive passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use successive metaphors to delineate anatomy or other detailed descriptions (examples: Xenophon, Plato's extended metaphors comparing body parts to citadel/isthmus/alleys). Employ sustained figurative chains to create vivid, life-like pictures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of excess in figurative language
rubrics_metrics.description: Figurative language has a constant tendency toward excess; overuse leads to feebleness, vapid trifling, and disgust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise restraint, especially with periphrasis and violent metaphors; critics (e.g., Caecilius) attack writers for intemperate language. Beware of inflated allegory and extravagant conceits that undermine authority and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off: loftiness with faults vs moderate flawlessness
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether sublimity accompanied by some faults should be preferred to a style never rising above moderate excellence but free of faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large intellects may neglect small details; great works may contain oversights but display greater excellences. The writer should weigh grandeur of soul and loftier excellences against occasional errors; evaluators should often vote loftiness to first place when greatness compensates for defects (examples: Homer vs Apollonius; Pindar/Sophocles vs their more decorous rivals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility, charm, and modest excellence vs sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Varied modulation, simplicity, touches of character, wit, polished raillery and well-bred irony contribute charm and make an author admirable, yet these do not necessarily constitute sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise the value of versatility (Hyperides' fluency, witty raillery, polished irony), but distinguish those qualities from true sublimity (Demosthenes lacks such charm but can be sublime). Do not conflate broad excellence and agreeableness with the loftiest literary rank.
